raw_comment: How in-depth the studies are and how planned the teachers are to teach the subjects, most are prepared with what they are going to teach and you can see their passion in the way they teach. There needs to be a standardised template for powerpoints and slides and also how they design moodle and where they place items. I have found that each course has different structures and settings and i am not sure if there has been a role out of powerpoints and slides that the teachers should be using?.
Knowledge / passion of teachers. The foreigner: australian student ratio is way too drastic. As an australian, I feel like I am studying in another country.
Placement.

I have completed some fascinating and engaging courses over the years that had some great teachers! I only completed one course this year which was just fine!. UNSW needs to fund its Arts Departments/ Degree. This course suffers from a lack of options and a very under resourced and underfunded staff. I think there is a lot of potential but it's clear that Arts is not valued at UNSW which is disappointing.

The flexibility of being able to pick elective subjects that align with my interests. Accessible resources and textbooks need to be more available. Having classes offered in more than one term. Trimesters not allowing for a depth of understanding a subject - it's too quick and feels like we just scratch the surface of every topic.
Going in placement and learning about the different disciplines of medicine. More practice exams for the biomed final at the end of this year.

Probably the tutorials and the interactive components where groups are able to share idea and learn off each other. The cost. The cost of classes has gone up significantly, especially during covid where the capacity to learn was greatly diminished.

The legal subjects are the best in this degree. It provides context and the reasons as to why the criminal justice system is the way it is. There needs to be more focus on other groups that touch the criminal justice system. There is far too much emphasis on First Nations people. Whilst there is justification for the inclusion of this group, they are not the only group. Basically I feel this is degree is an decolonising and First Nations people degree. I have spoken with many other students who all feel the same. The reality is that the criminal justice system touches many groups and all must be considered. This degree needs to be more diverse and inclusive. There are also many irrelevant subjects that were not clear where the topic was going. Also the constant 'reflecting' needs to be limited to one subject. It's repeated over and over in other subjects where students want to learn the material, no consistently 'reflect' on it. Critically analyse, yes, but not this constant circular 'reflecting'.
My exchange. Funding for the exchange. If a year exchange is compulsory, there should be a budget given to students instead of offering a $7000 loan they need to pay back indexed on hex.
The electives. Need to foster more of a sense of belonging.
My peers. The admin.

Classes where the professors were enthusiastic in teaching the course, and dedicated to helping to students to understand and apply these concepts to the industry. Some more direction for learning. Would be good to have better marking guidelines for assessments, and for examinations, to be given some/more practice questions related to the course, beyond typical course notes or tutorials.
Support from other research faculty, students and staff. More students participating in the program.
The friends/classmates I've met. The study spaces as it needs more quiet spaces and more spots with charging. The civil engineering building needs refurbishment.
The teachers! Amazing professors. The courses themselves, and the structure of the courses.
Detecting the use of AI. A professor wrongly accused me of using ChatGPT even when I had proof.

The lecturers that I had this year taught well, and also structured the course in a way that was easy to understand. Online resources were also easy to access and comprehensive, enabling remote study.My supervisors for my honours project were also extremely supportive and amazing to work with. Sometimes assessments were conducted at inappropriate hours.
The people I've met and the diversity of teachers. The structure of the assessments- less essays and more engaging work.
The wide variety of authors and theories we discuss. The freedom to focus on topics we are interested in. The structure of some courses are a bit convoluted.

The lecturers are always fantastic and are very passionate about their areas of study. I would say there should be more resources for theory students as we are the minority and do not use the practical spaces so it would be really useful if we had programs to understand the library system and areas were we can write and have support.
Really good teaching staff interesting courses fairly challenging. Nothing at the moment seems fair and good.
The part where I get to be a doctor at the end of it. The biomed campus days.
That you are creating content that can be used outside of class. Classes could be more shorter and more succinct. Repetition occurs a lot.

Attending lectures in person (this has been especially important to my study), the learning community I feel apart of in my tutorials and the friends I have made over the course of my study. Not cutting courses or general funding for the arts. This is a major problem for the ADA Faculty and the humanities in general. I have seen some of my excellent tutors be fired over the course of my degree, and their colleagues suffer that loss as a staff unit. The arts are imperative to the university, and the centre of all learning.
Flexibility, interesting, varied and diverse range of courses. Clarity around course progression.

The best aspects have been the field trips/lans/interactive classes where you are able to have a taste of field work. More interaction with the students in third year to give guidance on honours and career paths.

The ability to talk to and work with people I know who'll be very successful in their fields down the line. Probably the social cohesion aspect! Not being in block sections like Law students made it really hard for part-time workers like me to connect with people outside of societies, which weren't the type of people I'd get along with anyway.
The opportunity to connect with an audience in an exhibition. Studio spaces, course structures, expenses, resources provided and timeframes of final year subjects (too short).

Learning practical interviewing skills for clients, as this will be most relevant to jobs in clinical psychology. I also loved Prof. [specified name removed] [specified name removed] Honours elective workshop on The Psychology of Effective Presentations, I felt it was super engaging, class discussions were insightful, and the content was very relevant to everyday life. With the Honours year, there is no feedback on how you are ranked compared to your peers during the year, such as with the coursework. This makes it difficult for me to know how well I'm going, such as if I am on track for First Class, as I don't know where I sit compared to the cohort.
Meeting people and learning more about my program and how it can be applied to real life aspects and scenarios. Resources and accessibility.

Interesting electives that build on critical thinking skills and how to go about best science practice. Career development. It feels like if you don't get a first class mark during your honours year, you can't seem to go anywhere in psychology.
Being able to experience placement which has allowed for a practical element of learning. The fact that placement is not paid work makes it difficult for students who are not financially secure.
Learning interesting topics and meeting like minded people. Cramming too many topics into limited amount of time and lack of peer evaluation in group assessments.
Learning about self care, ethical reflection, and how to be a better listener. Ensure class participation from more than a handful of students.
Placement. Structure of courses (e.g. need longer lecture to cover all the content).
The diversity in courses. The inconsistency between course content with different lecturers and tutors.
N/a. No practical use, little to none skills learnt for job seeking, especially the marketing major.
Extracurricular bcom opportunities e.g., mentoring etc. Access to textbooks without having to pay extra on top of tuition feesInformation about majors and career opportunities of these.

The best part was honestly the whole philosophy faculty and the visual psychology team [specified name removed] [specified name removed] [specified name removed] etc). They are very understanding and accommodating as a deaf student. They teach in a way that is easy to understand and make accommodations for me that allow me to be comfortable. The fact that for the most part psychology final exams do not cover material in lectures and reference readings that we did not have. Also most of the profs (minus visual psych ones) have sucked at implementing my needs with my ELP like ensuring slides and information is up prior to lectures.
Open book assessments. Trimesters too high emphasis on class participation.
Trying new things. Relevance to career, skills needed in workplace.

Finding other who have similar mindsets to me and values. Also getting to be exposed to so many new lived experiences from others. The last year schedule needs improvement. The way that the classes for thesis is structured was not very helpful as many students are halfway through the thesis right now and we only just had a seminar of an intro to the thesis.

The passionate course convenors and instructions that have a lot of experience and wide range of knowledge that enjoy what they're teaching. The hands on work we get to participate in labs. The types of courses we do I find are not as relevant to our end career or provide us with much knowledge. I think it would be more helpful to do more anatomy courses not just learn about how to interact with people. I find a lot of courses can be quite repetitive from previous. Also the amount of weighting and types of assessment on some courses are ridiculous. Having to do multiple quizzes each week from 3 different courses plus multiple vivas and assessed pracs is so hard to manage. And the marking from some of the courses is very harsh when criteria is very broad and not explained well.
The teaching staff. Nothing that I can think of.

The best aspects of my program has been the wide selection of subjects within my degree. I have had the opportunity to study subjects related to the career I want to pursue in policy and analysis, whilst also challenging myself with the more mathematical elements and theory of economics as a whole. To improve I think there needs to be more incentive to attend classes and engage. Often class work is just going through homework questions where the solutions are released online afterwards. Beyond this, some of the subjects are way too content heavy and could be split up more evenly over the weeks.

Learning environment which includes friends and good facilities. Some lecturers are not helpful, some struggle to communicate and some set unrealistic standards when a whole class cannot achieve the task in a timeframe.
The tutors that are full of passion and help inspire you and push you to your potential. Better spaces for studio classes, e.g quality of air temp inside.
BABS faculty lecturers and Biological sciences labs. CHEM1011 teaching, CHEM1021 teaching and MATH1031 teaching. The subjects are not enjoyable and difficult to learn.
The internships and placements opportunity that UNSW has provided for us. None.

Clearer course outlines for some units - especially for assignment briefs and a clear guideline for a marking criteria for some units to ensure everyone is held to the same standard and there are minimal variables when marking.

The teaching staff are excellent. They are incredibly passionate and eager to help students both with the course work and with external areas of interest as well. Consistency. While I have been doing the degree, there has been a lot of changes which have made things more complicated and difficult than they should be at times.
The assessment have been well spaced out. The teachers need to come up with more innovative way to deliver content. No more just reading off PPT please.
The mandatory subjects should be removed. And lecturers should be more engaging.

The best aspects is that it is located at ADFA, which avoids many of the antisocial tendencies of most universities now a days. We desperately need more course options (at UNSW Canberra they have recently been cut back). I could barely do three courses of one major in a semester, and have decided to do all my mandatory courses this year in the hope that next year might actually have some of the courses that were advertised to me by the university when I accepted the offer.
Placement opportunities. Spread of content throughout all four years. Years one and two were not specific to exercise physiology at all.
Integrated learning, lots of group activities. Scheduling and structure of the course.
Engaging lecturers. More engaging tutorials less focus on assignments.
Being able to engage with people who are in the industry and giving there personal professional journey as it provides insight into what to expect once we graduate.
The campusThe coursesSome lecturers. Very repetitive ie: project charters, group charters.
The final 3rd year subjects actually feel applicable to the skills and knowledge needed for the workforce. Finding ways to bring the cohort together more.
Practical class.
Having tutors who have experience in the field, and them being very open to students asking questions and gaining support. Some tutors could be clearer on assignments, especially in the rubric.
Learning about a wide range of research topics. More help learning how to write certain assessments, especially in first year.

Decent structure and lecture recordings available. Use of online quizzes as an assessment is helpful. The assessments do tend to be fairly frequent and somewhat overwhelming and the large lectures make it hard to find people for groupwork if you do not have friends in that class.
I have enjoyed the variety of classes that I get to take. I enjoyed the opportunity for an internship, as well as learning from people who are currently working in research and social science fields.

Coming across passionate tutors who know they're course materials really well and teach it in a very easy format. Eg by making hard concepts easy to understand. The excessive use of group assignment which most cases negatively affects a students mark as they have to take on extra work and have group members that are a burden.
Professors and tutors having real industry experience in Journalism. Subjects need to be more diversified, often feel repetitive.
Some courses- Ability to choose electives and major. Structure of some courses.
Learning new skills. Teaching and course management.

The best aspects would be diving deeper into my chosen majors and having more time spent on learning about things I have interest in. The aspect that needs the most improvement would be the layout of the Moodle or chosen website courses are with. Sometimes the layout of the course is not well written with there being too much information in certain tabs.
Working with others. Teacher support.
Small cohort size at the rural campuses. Rural campuses don't get enough support from the lecturers and staff that are based in Sydney.

The structure of the law program is very well set out and the emphasis on class participation results in an excellent environment to learn in. I have found the assessments and content challenging but rewarding and feel like I am learning greatly beneficial things for my future career.

Getting to meet new people and experience more of uni life. Courses relating to my media degree have definitely changed the way I think about things and view life around me in a relatively positive way as well. It has been difficult starting uni post covid but since then I have developed a lot as a person, gotten much better at independent work and study and overall managing my time and life as a whole. The majority of the course was fine. I understand this course is no longer offered now and it was relatively confusing having to find out about this in my second year when I wanted to look at my classes. I think communication with the students could be better on course code changes and the discontinuation of degrees as it would have saved me lots of confusion and panic within that first year and a bit.

Learning about the content, a lot of the lectures or tutors are engaging and help you learn effectively. More experience clinically and having more placements earlier in the degree instead of till third year Some courses feel irrelevant and could've been replaced with more clinical experience and understanding.
The mixture of my degree and applying to my job. Some of the lecturers need to change and also some of the content is too focused on history and not practicality.

The best aspects were consistency in between courses in terms of assignments so That I can apply what I've learnt in other courses to the work I'm doing in present and future courses. The lecture recordings should be more consistent in terms of quality and mandating the lecturers to use the mic at all times even if the few attending could hear them. I also believe that the assignments should be communicated more clearer intents of the rubric with more details instead of generic criteria.

Interacting with different people studying different things. Learning a lot of soft skills that I can't develop well in engineering alone. Some courses seem to be vague and have little direction in what exactly they are trying to teach. Some courses had lots of class discussions and were interactive but had little content to learn.

The program covers a wide range of specialities that have given me a good understanding of what specific field I might like to go into in the workforce. It has been a challenging yet rewarding program so far. There isn't anything that comes to mind instantly, as the course is generally structured well. If anything, it can be difficult to plan out what electives to choose as UNSW has trimesters, and some courses are only offered for one out of three terms during a year.
Having sufficient time to learn instead of cramming so much information.

Meeting friends that I've maintained since Stage 1 and being able to meet/study together in and out of class with them throughout my studies.Some demonstrators/tutors were very nice, approachable and helpful. Some lecturers were difficult to understand as recorded lectures didn't include captions or the lecture slides didn't contain enough information.

Hybrid mix of classes online and in campus helps manage lifestyle with work and study. Assessment and course outlines. More online options for classes. Less free electives when doing a single major or greater business choices for free electives such as management or banking basics courses.
Self and independent learning and learning to communicate. Consistency across studios.

Meeting new people, learning in the labs and utilising proper equipments and working with cadavers. The structure of some courses need to be changed to fit one trimester (10 weeks) instead of fitting into one of two semesters (14 weeks). I would also like more feedback on my assignments as the lecturers simply marked based on the marking rubric instead of showing me how I'd actually get a higher marks or where I missed out on marks.
Mates and colleagues, having collaborative activities. Group stuff. Good grades. Realistic test prep. More guidance, especially if it is a 3rd yr student doing a 4th yr subject.

The course structure has been good, and having online classes allows my timetable to be more flexible. It hard to transition from online to face to face so suddenly. This has been the hardest past that I have experienced, as most classes have now become in person.
Getting to study a diverse range of different design disciplines in my one degree. Very hands on studios. Studio classes are too long, studio classes are often too similar with their brief.

Industry placements are the best part, gives me exposure to the real world, teaches corporate etiquette and shapes my direction of what I want to do in the future. Most of the courses don't teach us any important hard skill. Just lots of fancy words building on common sense.
Helpful lecturers and tutors for all of my classes. Proving more feedback for assignments and getting results back in a timely manner.

The best aspect about my program is the internships they provide at industry leaders allowing us to develop work related skills that are essential for the work force. The most improvement that the program requires is communicating with the students more in an informal setting such as little catch ups with different streams.

The collaborative aspect of it. My courses have often required creativity, which I have enjoyed participating in with other students. The level of teaching varies quite drastically. Some tutors are amazing and genuinely care about the course and our learning, whilst others are very disengaged and barely teach.

Learning more about Medical Science in general, and the content relevant to my future career path. Additionally, the content I have learnt has also been interesting to me as well, which has been another positive aspect. The course is very well structured and all the required courses are relevant to the degree, so I am unsure what should be improved.

The different majors provided, very broad learning areas that are interesting. Workload isn't demanding and it's easy to catch up on content. Content can be a bit repetitive sometimes and the real life applications are lacking a bit. Across courses the content can overlap so it feels like a waste of money. Also a lot of group work in B.Com, often with international students where it is harder to communicate effectively. Less weighting on group tasks would be good.

Being able to connect with like minded people and expand my learning on a greater level. Being able to learn and do things ive never done before is amazing. I cant think of anything much for media, im very happy with it.

The facilities and having access to many different studio spaces for practice. I also enjoy the environment of the Paddington campus and the way it fosters a positive and welcoming attitude in both students and staff. I feel that some improvement needs to be made with accessing some spaces. e.g. it is often difficult to gain access to spaces allocated by the resource centres. (e.g. the film development labs and the 2 hour slots - this then is complicated as the space is often very full, making it difficult to produce work).
Degree needs to be more streamlined. Need more opportunities to meet people doing the same degree, as it's very hard to do so on a daily basis.

I love that many course and concepts somewhat link together. Also, I like how it practices public speaking. More enthusiastic, engaging and knowledgeable lecturers/tutors need to be brought in. Instead of implementing compulsory lectures, tackle the issue of absentees by introducing educators who are actually passionate and know what they're teaching. - Many lecturers tend to just waffle to reach the 2 hours mark.- There needs to be a better support system for studies, as PASS classes are usually held when I'm in another INFS class.- There is too much weighing on group tasks for every single course. This means my WAM tanks as a result of freeloaders in my group, which is hard to avoid since we don't know each other when we first start the course.- There is a lack of community in Information Systems. Educators do not facilitate activity in a space where students should be comfortable to speak up on forums and engage with other peers socially.- CoP needs to be removed. Participation marks are immensely subjective and tutors never really record such engagement. The implementation of these marks force students to waste tutorial time on making random statements that every student who has at least attended the lecture or read the slides already knows.Overall, I feel that there is no existing sense of community and willing/natural engagement in and outside the classroom for the Information Systems program. - For reference, Computer Science has a great forum community with students who are passionate for programming, due to enthusiastic professors. They also have many study and employability support systems.

The degree has a wide range of classes you are able to choose from which allows me to explore fields I am more passionate about. Further, due to its flexibility, I am able to choose classes and courses that match with my own schedule and interests. Some aspects that need the most improvement would be the teamwork skills in the course. As most economic courses are focused on more independent work, it would be nice to see a little bit more of team assignments to build our teamwork skills.

The best aspects of the degree have been the courses that I can tell have course coordinators that put in a lot of care and effort into organising and considering the cohort's mental. Being able to experience these courses is the highlight of my degree as it makes my learning as streamlined and comfortable as possible. I think having courses that all mostly use moodle instead of mixed platforms would be better as sometimes it can be difficult to track information.

When hands on learning is provided. One of the courses it was very hard to practice for exams as the exams were practical, we only had access to those labs during class time where we had to learn and very few optional labs which made it really hard to study for a exam worth 50% of the course.
Friendly staff. Meeting and connecting with other students.

The best aspects are probably the students you meet along the way, since we study very similar degrees we are able to assist each other in class and have bonding moments over similar courses. I have also really appreciated certain tutors, while few, have gone above and beyond in their teaching. The aspects that need the most improvement includes the courses. A lot of the courses combine a multitude of different majors which results in a lack on in-depth exploration of any. Many courses feel like they lack a solid focus and typically only focus on theory which does not offer any real world application or even useful skills.

The cohort is rather small so I have had the opportunity to form connections to most of the people within it. Classes, especially studio classes, really do promote a sense of community and group learning so I really do feel like part of a close knit community. I think that some of the classes have been challenging in that their delivery was not clear whether it be confusing assessment briefs or convoluted noodle pages. Additionally, Architecture can be very expensive when taking into account the cost of printing large A0 panels or model making. I think an improvement in those facilities: e.g. ensuring that there are more than 2 large format printers and that they don't break/don't charge us if the panels don't print.

My MATH2400 lecturer [specified name removed] [specified name removed] and being put in a situation where I have to challenge myself to grow as a person. Needs to have more interactions between lecturers and students, and they need to provide more support to their students (i.e replying to emails faster, providing help to students with assignments and exams in a non-judgmental way), making it less stressful and anxiety driven for students to pass (i.e. removing or becoming more lenient with a 40% final exam pass hurdle).
Learning new skills and content. Course does not allow much flexibility with classes , many in person classes that require students to attend uni 4 days a week in person.

Lecturers from the Nutrition/ Dietetics program itself [specified name removed] and [specified name removed] are very enthusiastic and fantastic lecturers. They are succinct, easy to understand and easy to approach. Lecturers from other courses are not as easy to understand, and pacing of subjects is not great. Pacing of some subjects is very fast and hard to stay on top of. This is most likely due to the trimester structure of UNSW. Additionally, some of the subjects in the course felt like they were irrelevant in the professional field of nutrition/dietetics. Some subjects didn't feel relevant and I struggled to identify how it could develop my professional career.

The ability to integrate internships as part of my degree gives me the opportunity to apply learnings in the actual workplace, and better understand what the career entails. Some of the organisation of certain classes and internship requirements could be improved, due to a general difficulty to locate and access certain resources.
Possibly the extra-curriculars and integrated learning whilst i did my degree. The workload is too much for a 3 course term.

The best aspects of the Bachelor of Design program was definitely the social aspect. The cohort and structure of the class encouraged social engagement and allows students to easily network. The structure of classes and assessments needs to be reevaluated, the electives/ specialisations of classes are quite good and intuitive, but a lot of the general education classes are quite repetitive and need major improvement as assessment tasks and content is quite repetitive and hard to integrate into your portfolio and professional space. I also would suggest to add an internship unit, or more units with how to integrate yourself into the industry as a student.
The courses and electives offer a wide array of different subjects. The teachers, some can be rude and quick.
Content is very interesting and practical. More organised.
The people and learning community. Enrolment processes most of the engineering courses are full.

Learning from industry experts and having insight of how theory plays out in social work practice. Ensuring that all students are contributing equally to group assignments and are actively involved in design of group assessments.
Being able to learn more about content that I am passionate about. The assignments and explanations of content as it can be quite rushed.

Consistency, focus on education and improving student understanding rather than reducing workload for staff, providing feedback, more transparency in marking process, better handling of grievances, especially those made against staff.

The organisation of resources on my unsw and moodle. Easy to find information for each course in the course outline and the set of moodle has been helpful in navigating assessments and course requirements. Although the tutors are very educated and intelligent, some tutors don't seem to harness the ability to teach which can be difficult to learn these complex ideas.
The online lectures. The biweekly quizzes so you stay on track and up to date. The final exam being weighed so heavily and the compulsory in person labs.

The freedom to study my interest and the level of support and mentorship from the faculty. At times, the organisation of courses need improvement as they can be hard to follow, particularly on moodle.
Learning environment. Nothing.
The structure of teaching. More clinical work in year 1 and 2.
Learning what I am interested in. Course structure.
Rural clinical school.

The tutors and convenors are beneficial, caring, considerate, and knowledgeable. I feel that I have learned a lot from them as well as my fellow students. It's been a joyful time of learning and developing my skills and knowledge. More financial assistance during placement. It was a very stressful time as student.

The best aspects have been the support and engagement from tutors and educators. You feel like part of a community and everyone is passionate about their own and others work. I have progressed so much this year and it is all thanks to the excellent tutor engage, help and program structure. I am grateful for the opportunity and space to try so many different disciplines and techniques to making and the facilities and resources are so foundational to make that reality!. Hard question. I would probably say the expenses of providing your own materials for a lot of subjects. It can become very expensive on the side of paying for mandatory material kits. But the reduced student prices for machines and equipment is very helpful.
The knowledgeable tutors and faculty peers. It needs more relevant to life experience rather than the history.
Learning new concepts. Took a finance and accounting topic last term. Very engaging and interesting. No issues so far.

In-person learning is quite prioritised, which has been excellent - e.g. no recorded videos like my previous degree in science, more emphasis on coming to lectures and tutorial on campus. Some of the teaching. Courses don't feel like they can be challenging enough - something to do with trimester format, possibly, with the limit on the number of assessments. So in a couple of courses it has felt like we aren't being tested according to the knowledge / content being taught...

Hands on/ field work components tied to an assessment because they feel the most relevant to working in industry and equipping me with both the technical and people based skills I need to excel in the workplace post University. Maybe inclusion of more industry visits and guest lecturers discussing careers after uni to not only motivate students but make the content feel a little more real world applicable.

Honestly, my favourite part of my degree program is the diversity of learning. Throughout the required and suggested courses in my degree, I've been able to learn about sociology, psychology and international politics as well as social work itself. Not only does this allow me a more diverse education, but gives me a wider breadth of knowledge to apply to my future work as a social worker. I've also been able to meet and befriend people from a wide array of backgrounds, which feels special to me as someone from a small and homogenous country town. Overall, I'm extremely happy with the course. Something that could maybe be improved is the fact that coursework is often shared across required courses, which can contribute to a sense of repetition.

SocialAcademicNew experiencesAccess to volunteering. Field trips in courses which are already incredibly expensive in an increasingly expensive world cost hundreds of dollars. The food and campsites included are not worth hundreds of dollars, and transport is often not included. Tuition is already being paid for. Excess fees like this are unfair.
It is engaging because of its smaller class , instead of the a larger cohort. Overall i think that 11 weeks of learning isn't enough for one course it felt rushed.

Interacting with people who are in the field themselves was very memorable for me. it was interesting to see how they applied their experiences while teaching. At times, the way that the courses are structured are convoluted, either due to there being too many assignments or them not being explained concisely enough.

The opportunity to meet new people and learn content concerning diverse topics (data, finance, accounting). More directly applicable to work; many of the courses seem designed only to unnecessarily lengthen the degree.
The amount of major assignments are fair. Some advanced courses require prerequisite knowledge which makes it disadvantageous for the students who did not study prior to the subject.

The best aspects of the Bachelor Degree of Science are the assessment tasks, especially the mobius-based tests which relieve the pressure of the final exam. Aspects of the program that need most improvement is that there should be group tasks as it allows more social interaction within the classes.

Being able to meet new people and people who I have been able to remain friends with over the last couple of terms. For me personally I found it a little bit frustrating that most of the courses for my major wasn't offered till the last term.
AVIA1111 and flight selection. Relevance of some courses such as science communication and the math courses.

I enjoyed learning about finance and micro economics also there is a lower in person time commitment plus work load when compared to my other degree (engineering) which meant I was able to focus more on the more time demanding subjects whilst not sacrificing my commitment to commerce courses. Some of the courses feel unrelated/ unstructured e.g comm1120 is about collaboration. Whilst I feel this is important I feel it should not be a mandatory course.

The course layout, help from the nucleus student hub in working out what to do and how to schedule classes, flexibility, some lecturers. Some organisation/ clarity in some courses that may be be less organised than others, learning how to self direct learning and manage study schedule.

Learning chemistry and biology that's relevant for me in the futureMeeting people that have similar interests in my program Interacting with lecturers who are enthusiastic about their contentHaving some food related subjects so I can learn the fundamentals of food rather than only doing scienceGreat course lead who inspired me to stay in dietetics and make this my career. Some courses we've taken definitely need to be organised better It would be nice if we could choose some electives cause it's nice for all the graduates to have some different qualities they've developed.
Developing new skills and views, meeting new people, interactive with and learning from tutors. Support outside of classroom.
Meeting new people and being able to do experiments and understand certain topics. N/a.
Being introduced to new forms of thinking and a vast variety of literature. Delving deeper into readings in tutorials.

I honestly enjoyed a particular course (COMM1110) which taught us the basics of Excel, a relevant tool for my future career. Relevance. The First Year Integrated Course structure at UNSW feels like a huge gamble for money, I would have never wanted to pursue it at UNSW if I knew I would be taking subjects like COMM1150 which bear very little relevance to what I want to do. It's a waste of time, I'd rather jump straight into majors rather than being forced to pay through the nose for a year to learn subjects that are just common sense apart from a few.

From my experience as a student with a neurological disability, staff have all been very understanding and considerate towards my condition and tried to help me in the ways that they could. Even if situations did not go well for me, I could tell that most of them had good intentions. The program in regards to structure and timing is quite inflexible. Often times, lectures and tutorials are only held at one timing per week, meaning students have to reorganise their daily timetables and activities to revolve around uni. This is quite inconvenient for students who have jobs or other appointments during the day, or students who live far from campus and have to commute, as they cannot select alternate class timings to suit them. In addition to this, the overall program is very structured, with lots of courses that require the completion of prerequisite courses. However, sometimes, only specific courses are offered during the term. This means that if students were to slightly differ from the sample program layout, their future progression could be significantly affected. In my case, with my disability, I struggle a lot with the heavy workload and find it hard to get good grades when taking all of the required courses. Yet, the consequences of dropping a single course could stunt my course enrollment for the following terms. Another aspect of the program that affected me is communication with staff. With my condition, I am granted learning adjustments to have more flexibility around task deadlines, but only upon agreement with the course convener. During the year, some of my conveners were very responsive, which really helped me. But some did not respond to my emails in time, or at all, which not only affected my stress levels, but also prevented me from having my extensions implemented and thus impacted my performance and grades in certain tasks.

Moreover, my lecturers often fail to be concise. This is important for helping students stay engaged, model good communication skills (lecturers often desire concise writing in essays - written communication), and to avoid wasting time. Contact hours, I believe, have the potential to be one of the more intellectually stimulating and otherwise beneficial ways of digesting course content and spurring critical thinking (for example, because of the instant feedback and correction a lecturer is able to provide to students, or the relative ease with which the lecturer can pass on a passion for learning, and thus inspire future knowledge production). This year in particular I do believe that the course content has been aimed at teaching us more 'real world' applications of the industry which has been great. However, what I believe could and should be improved is the structure and expected deliverables for our courses each semester. Currently with the trimester structure there are 3 assessments per course. I have had 3 courses each semester meaning that each semester I have at least 9 assessments to complete. In some cases some courses have two parts to an assignment with a sizeable amount of work for each part. An example of this was semester 2, where we had 3 subjects, 3 assessments for each with the exception of 1 subject wherein for 2 of the assessments it had two parts to the assignment meaning that this course alone had 5 assessments on top of the other two courses that we had bringing the total number of assessments to 11 assessments to complete in a semester of 10 weeks. This paired with the assessment schedule which had assessment clashes and different assessments for different subjects placed one after the other made it a very difficult semester which created a lot of pressure inside and outside of uni. I strongly believe that the best solution to this problem which occurs almost every semester is to change the structure from 3 assessments per course to 2. This would create a more positive work environment for students as well as tutors and convenors and would allow for students to produce a higher resolution of work as they would have more time to complete the work.

I am incredibly fortunate to benefit from the world-class resources available to us, both through the dedicated staff at UNSW and the extensive materials provided by the library. What has truly stood out to me is how this degree has deepened my passion for health and exercise. Every tutorial, practical session, and resource has expanded my knowledge, equipping me with the skills and insights I need to succeed in the field of physiotherapy. I am deeply grateful for the countless opportunities that UNSW has offered, from state-of-the-art facilities to academic and professional support. These experiences have solidified my confidence in pursuing my career and have made my educational journey deeply fulfilling. While the degree at UNSW is exceptional in many respects, I believe there is room for improvement in terms of timetable flexibility and class scheduling. One of the challenges I've faced is the difficulty in balancing university commitments with work. With classes scheduled across four days a week, often at times that don't allow for a full day of work, it can be hard to manage both academic responsibilities and the need to support myself financially.The current schedule, with classes sometimes spread out or held at awkward times, leaves little room for meaningful work hours, especially for those who need to sustain themselves or save for the future while studying. Greater flexibility in timetables whether through offering more online classes, consolidating in-person sessions into fewer days, or providing evening or weekend options would make a significant difference. As students, many of us are juggling multiple commitments, including part-time jobs, internships, and extracurricular activities, all of which are essential for both our personal growth and professional development. A more flexible approach would allow us to maintain a healthier balance between study, work, and personal time, making it easier to apply our education to real-world experiences and opportunities without compromising either. I believe that such improvements would not only enhance the overall student experience but also contribute to better mental and financial well-being.

The Bachelor of Data Science and Decisions program is structured in a way that gives students a well-rounded perspective. One aspect I particularly appreciate is the interdisciplinary nature of the program. This has opened my eyes to the vast potential of data science and how it can influence everything from business and technology to mathematics and beyond. The Bachelor of Data Science and Decisions program could benefit from improvements in several key areas. First, there is a noticeable lack of student engagement, particularly within the data science cohort. Building a stronger sense of community among students could greatly enhance the learning experience, as collaboration and networking are crucial in this field. Organizing more interactive events, study groups, or workshops could help foster a more engaged and connected student body.Additionally, the availability of student counseling is quite limited. Given the complexity of the coursework and the wide array of career paths available in data science, having more accessible academic and career guidance would be highly beneficial. This would help students better navigate their academic journey and make more informed decisions about their specializations and career trajectories.Lastly, I think the program could integrate more hands-on, real-world projects. While the theoretical knowledge is valuable, more practical experience with real data and industry-related problems would prepare students for the workforce more effectively. This could be achieved through partnerships with industry professionals, internships, or collaborative projects with businesses and organizations.

The textbook can be a reference but should not be used to perfunctorily teach students. We need not only theory but also practical case studies. X has a gift; his passion for the subject matter shines through, and is infectious. He has the ability to imbue otherwise dry content with the requisite enthusiasm to engage even the most burnt-out undergrad.
This is in part due to his passion, in part due to his preparation, and in no small part his encyclopaedic understanding of the course – delivering insight with dry wit (which doubles as a good revision mnemonic).
He is extraordinarily knowledgeable on the subject matter – enough to frequently offer relevant trivia (making for particularly handy dinner table conversational fodder). Demonstrated through his ability to explain complex and sophisticated international law concepts in clear, cogent terms – X makes tractable areas of law that have claimed the scalps of far more ambitious students in terms past.
X clearly cares for his students, and this goes a long way in facilitating their engagement; with the tenderness of interacting with an oft-neglected shelter dog, X teaches with sufficient compassion to coax students into trusting that they won’t suffer at the cruel hands of public law once more.
Whilst it can’t be measured through MyExperience, the strongest anecdotal testament to X’s teaching is the number of students who, prior to taking this course, considered international law ‘bullshit’; because of X, many are now considering a career in this field. From a jaded law student, this is one of the highest possible accolades.
Furthermore, the delivery of this unit comes at a particularly interesting time; with the ongoing conflict(s) in the Middle East, the recent ICJ rulings, ICC warrants – there is much overlap between current events and course themes/content. As a Jewish student, there was much apprehension (both personally, and in the wider community) around taking this course in the current circumstances. X has navigated these circumstances with grace and class – he has facilitated important, meaningful, and relevant conversations around events/concepts with appropriate sensitivity. Most importantly, he has done so in a way that does not stymie discussion, nor preclude those from feeling like they can engage – irrespective of their political priors. This is in contrast to some feedback I have heard from students in other classes; it is a difficult feat to achieve, and X ought to be commended for it.
X is an excellent educator; it is quite clear he has many opportunities available to him. The UNSW Law community is far richer for his decision to work here.

What could be improved:
• Several old articles that are a hard read, and lacked narrative.
• The activities throughout the course do not relate to the assessment or discussion forums.
• There is a lot of readings on general technology, less on models, concepts and theory.
• Although I thought it was straightforward, there was confusion from students on the alternative posting for group A or B. This should be plain to understand from week 1.
• Students did not realise they needed to post audio/visual content. Suggest using audio/visual content in your opening posts so students follow.
• Applying full Harvard referencing style in posts kills the chat vibe. In my mind, the forums are a replacement for students talking in a breakout.
• Assessment 2 is quite descriptive by nature. The questions refer to models that are not related to the course, e.g. Porters Five Forces is not in Unit 1-10, yet it is a question in the assessment (why?).
• The questions in the forums don't lead to strong debate, again, they lead to a descriptive responses. e.g. describe scrum or CICD. This led to 20 posts starting with similar answers.
What did not go well:
• Most assessments allow students to deep dive into concepts. Assessment 4 does not allow students to interact with the lessons learnt from Units 1-10 effectively. More of an extension from the Marketing course in the MBA rather than a technology investigation.
• Word limits were not enforced or respected in posts. In fairness, writing 200-500 words, some of it rambling, is significantly easier than attempting to write a succinct 100 or 200 word post.
• Very detailed specific referencing requirements. In other courses, the lecturer has provided a simple one pager of what they expect for referencing. Problem solved. If the feedback to students is they should reference the UNSW Harvard referencing guide. Then I would suggest looking into the disparity of referencing syntax between Unit 6 and Unit 10. I went looking for a standard and could not find one.
• I suspect Assessment 3 is susceptible to AI. Although the lecturers can only mark what is in front of them, it would be easy to spot outliers in the data, whereby students that received credit for all assessments then achieve 100% in their exam. I really like exams. However, this weakness should be pause for thought on its future applicability.
• Reading 5.5 is long, industry specific and dated, there are many great alternative videos and articles on Blockchain. As is Reading 10.8.

I understand that the purpose of the course was to incorporate as much policy/critque as possible to encourage students to think deeply about whether the law should be the way it is, but for a course like this - which can make or break a graduate seeking to practice law - I think there should be a much stronger focus on the substantive law as it is.
I quite like the theory/critique components of the course, but I think the way the textbook is written makes it incomrehensibly dense and difficult. For e.g. the discussions on X was painful to sit through and the theory/critique just blended in with the 'substantive' parts of the readings. I would have liked to see a stronger and clearer separation to the effect of "Here's the law - and now here's why it's shit" so that engagement with the theory is made more meanigful. Basically, I think you should be given a firm grasp of what the law is so that it's easier for you to spot the cracks and appreciate the deficiencies.
More on the textbook:
- It makes a mockery of my time. For e.g. there was a substantial portion of the Judicial warning chapter dedicated to what the Roman Law on 'proofs' was. I get why the topic was explored but the matter should have been highlighted by way of a well-placed footnote or two and a link to further reading for those that are interested and have the time for it.
- The textbook also runs around and between concepts like a headless chicken. Sure, evidence can be relevant for more than one purpose but I don't think the matter should have been taught through the lens of hearsay examples. Something like relevance is meant to be the simpler part of evidence law and also its core foundation - keep it as simple as it can be. [See also readings on proof - why was the Prasad direction and its abandonment discussed before the student had a chance to fully appreciate what BARD actually entails? How is the student meant to understand why the evidence wasn't capable of meeting the Crown's standard of proof when they hadn't yet read about what that standard of proof even is?]
- The structure of the textbook and course - I understand why the course decided to teach Pt 3.11 right after Pt 3.1 but why jump to Credibility right after? And WHY cover Character before tendency, coincedence and crucially, Opinion? s 111 was entirely useless to me until i later covered expert opinion readings. Similarly the readings for Character dintinguishing tendency and context evidence was unbelievably frustrating since I hadn't covered those concepts properly. There's a reason why the ALRC and NSWLRC organised the Act in the way they did after spending a decade or so on it. Please don't dilly dally around with it when there seems to be no good reason for it (unlike with teaching Pts 3.1 and 3.11 first)

The following feedback will be about the forum which applies to all course admins and teachers on the forum including X.
The forum could be used more effectively. The answers to forum questions have been far too unhelpful or vague. I agree that if there is a direct and specific answer to the question in one of our resources such as the ICL, lectures or consultation sessions, that students should be directed towards these resources instead. However, when directing students, please give them the specific time stamp for lectures and consultation sessions or the specific topic/week/section for the ICL. Most of the responses, with very few exceptions, ask students to simply watch the recording of the consultation session or go back to the ICL. This is very discouraging as most likely the student has already used these resources and want further help/clarification or they have to sift through every detail of the resource to find a broad answer which is very inefficient and defeats the purpose of the forum.
Further, when asked to explain a specific question, please don't ask students to simply go read/watch the answers to a similar question, unless their question is specifically and accurately answered in a video/solutions. Even then, student's might need further help. During the learning process, often slight changes to a similar branch of questions can be confusing for student's and they need the extra assistance to bridge these gaps in their knowledge. The forum is a great way to get personalised responses or feedback to questions as everyone will interpret a question differently if not guided correctly.
I understand that tutors and course admins spend a lot of time creating resources to help students and that it would be a waste to not use these. However, most students ask questions based on the content or questions we are provided. By nature, most questions will always be somehow related to the content that the course provides. From what i've experienced, if it's a question that is related to content, students will be redirected to the course content again. This leaves the forum to only be open to questions that aren't extensively covered in or related to the course, which essentially reduces the effectiveness of forums. Redirecting the student's to an upcoming consultation is fair, but there will be cases where some student's questions don't get answered or don't get answered well. In those cases the forum should be useful.
Therefore if a question hasn't been answered before it would benefit student's greatly if admins could answer to each student's specific questions in detail or redirecting them specifically to where their question will be accurately answered and not broadly. I kindly suggest these improvements to the forum because I have seen it implemented in other courses and I have found them to enrich my learning.

There are a few things that could be improved from personal experience.
1. Course Content and Structure
Personally, the intention to teach multiple aspects of Performance at an introductory level did not really work well for me. I felt like we did not go deep enough into each topic to learn about it and that there was no synthesis between each week. It was hard to draw a link between each lecture topic and it felt like we are floating between classes without cementing our knowledge.
Moreover, there was not much "intention" in the lecture content. It felt like a mash-up of different people's voices instead of one authorial voice making sense of them. The lecture content often included quotes, videos and excerpts from a variety of sources that did not necessarily unify to emphasise a strong message.
It may be better if there is a better structure in each lecture where we know exactly how the topic is divided into its sub-topics and how we are going to link them back together, similar to what we've done in Week's 2 Lecture -- Breaking, slide 3.
In addition, it may be beneficial if there was better synthesis between each topic. This will bring better cohesion to the course and more catharsis after the whole course is taught.
2. Balance between Practicality and Theory
Given that the final assessment was a 3-5 minute performance, I was surprised at the lack of prac in our tutorials. We spent the majority of the time sitting down, discussing different topics and listening to insights about that week's content.
In order to relate the assessments better to the course itself, it might be advantageous to do more practical work in our tutorials -- allowing us to explore different forms of performance first-hand, and consequently get a better understanding of what we'd like to do for our performance.
